findings.title: applyDiscount accepts unbounded or non-numeric price and pct
findings.description: applyDiscount({ price, pct }) computes price - (price * pct) / 100 with no check that price is a finite non-negative number or that pct is within 0..100. A pct above 100 or negative yields a negative or inflated line price, and non-numeric input yields NaN. Today the only call path passes pct as the constant 0, so it is not currently attacker-reachable; the risk appears once ticket 501 feeds pct or price from request data.
findings.attackPath: src/export.js:10 (items taken from req.body.items) -> src/export.js:15 total(items, 0) -> src/cart.js:3 applyDiscount(item.price, pct) -> src/price.js:2 arithmetic on unvalidated values. pct is the constant 0 at export.js:15, so only price is attacker-influenced today. Once pct is request-controlled, the same path gives negative totals.
findings.exploit: After a discount source is wired in, a client sends pct=150 or a negative price on a cart line so the computed total drops below zero or to a favourable value. Not run.
findings.mitigationExamined: Looked for validation in price.js, cart.js, export.js and server.js and found none. pct is hard-coded to 0 at export.js:15, which blocks exploitation at present. No authentication or authorization layer exists in server.js.
findings.fix: Validate in applyDiscount: require Number.isFinite(price) && price >= 0 and Number.isFinite(pct) && pct >= 0 && pct <= 100, and throw otherwise. Take the discount percentage from server-side configuration or a trusted record, never from the request body. Compute money in integer minor units.

findings.category: Insecure remote code execution (curl | sh) / unverified download
findings.title: setup.sh pipes a remote installer straight into sh with no integrity check
findings.description: The setup script runs `curl -fsSL https://get.example-reports.dev/install.sh | sh`. The downloaded script is executed immediately, unverified (no checksum, signature or pinned version), and no `set -e`/pipefail guards against a truncated download being executed. `-L` follows redirects and `--proto '=https'` is not set, so a redirect downgrade to http is not blocked.
findings.attackPath: package.json:6 (`npm run setup` -> `sh scripts/setup.sh`) -> scripts/setup.sh:3 curl fetches https://get.example-reports.dev/install.sh -> piped into `sh` at scripts/setup.sh:3, executing whatever the remote host serves with the privileges of the invoking user.
findings.exploit: An attacker who compromises or takes over get.example-reports.dev (host, DNS, certificate, or the vendor's release pipeline), or who obtains a redirect or downgrade, serves a malicious install.sh. The next developer or provisioning job that runs `npm run setup` executes it, giving arbitrary code execution on a developer machine or fresh server (possibly as root) with access to source, credentials and the network. A truncated response would also run a partial script.
findings.mitigationExamined: HTTPS gives transport confidentiality and server authentication, and `-f` aborts on HTTP errors. There is no checksum, signature, version pin or content verification. The script is not an npm lifecycle hook (package.json:6 only defines a manual `setup` script), so it is not triggered by `npm install`; this limits exposure to deliberate invocations and is why the rating is Medium rather than High.
findings.fix: Download a versioned installer to a file, verify a pinned SHA-256 or signature, then execute it; or install through a pinned package manager or lockfile. Use `curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2`, add `set -eu`, and avoid running it as root.

findings.title: Sole HTTP entry point routes every request to the export handler with no authentication, authorization or input gate
findings.description: server.js creates a bare node:http server whose only handler forwards every request, on any method and path, to exportCart. Nothing authenticates the caller, checks a role, ties the requested report name to the caller's own record, or validates the request before it reaches the handler. The handler (src/export.js:11-12) takes req.query.name and concatenates it into a shell command and into the report file path.
findings.attackPath: src/server.js:3 (any request, no auth) -> src/export.js:9 exportCart(req, res) -> src/export.js:11 name = req.query.name -> src/export.js:12 exec('zip -q /tmp/' + name + '.zip /var/reports/' + name + '.csv') -> shell. A name containing shell metacharacters runs arbitrary commands, and one with ../ reads other customers' report files.
findings.exploit: An unauthenticated client sends GET /export?name=x;<command>;# (URL-encoded) to the server. Once req.query exists, the shell runs the injected command, and the response returns the zipped report name and cart total. A name such as ../other-customer/report selects another customer's report, with no ownership check in server.js.
findings.mitigationExamined: No authentication or authorization middleware, no router, no allow-list or validation exists in server.js or export.js. The only thing in the way is accidental: exportCart uses Express-only APIs (req.query, res.status, res.set, res.json) on plain node:http objects, and package.json has no express dependency. req.query is therefore undefined and the handler throws before exec runs, so as wired today the sink is not reached.
findings.fix: Put an authentication step and an authorization check in front of the handler, deriving the customer from the session or token rather than the request and checking the report belongs to them. Route explicitly on method and path (GET /export only) and return 404 otherwise. Validate name against a strict pattern such as ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$. In export.js replace the exec string with execFile or an archiving library with an argument array, and resolve the path under /var/reports and confirm it stays inside. Use one consistent framework (or add the missing one) so req.query and res.json exist.

findings.title: Unsanitised query parameter concatenated into a shell command in exportCart
findings.description: exportCart builds a shell command string with the request's `name` query parameter and runs it with child_process.exec, which invokes a shell. No validation, escaping or argument-array API is used. The handler is written for a framework that exposes req.query; server.js's bare node:http server does not, so the flaw is latent in the current wiring and live once the handler is mounted on such a framework, as the GET /export?name= comment intends.
findings.attackPath: src/server.js:3 (http.createServer routes every request to exportCart) -> src/export.js:11 (name = req.query.name, attacker-controlled) -> src/export.js:12 (exec('zip -q /tmp/' + name + '.zip /var/reports/' + name + '.csv'))
findings.exploit: Request GET /export?name=x;<command>%20%23 so the shell runs the injected command after zip, as the service user. No authentication is required. Described only, never run.
findings.mitigationExamined: No input validation, allow-list, quoting or execFile usage anywhere in the path; server.js adds no auth or routing; no framework default sanitises query values. The only condition is that req.query must be populated by a framework, which the node:http server does not do today.
findings.fix: Do not build a shell string. Validate name against a strict allow-list such as /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$/, then use child_process.execFile('zip', ['-q', outPath, inPath]) with no shell, or use an in-process zip library. Require authentication and derive the report path from the caller's identity.

findings.title: Partner API bearer token is sent back to the requesting client in a response header
findings.description: On success, exportCart calls res.set('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + PARTNER_API_TOKEN), which sets a header on the HTTP response to the caller. The comment says the data goes to the partner, but nothing is sent to the partner; the credential is handed to whoever called the endpoint. The same latent-wiring condition as the injection finding applies. The hard-coded literal itself is left to the secrets lane.
findings.attackPath: src/server.js:3 (any request) -> src/export.js:12 (zip succeeds, err is null) -> src/export.js:14 (res.set('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + PARTNER_API_TOKEN)) -> response headers to the caller
findings.exploit: An unauthenticated client requests /export with a name that makes zip succeed and reads the Authorization response header to obtain the live partner token, then uses it against the partner API. Described only, never run.
findings.mitigationExamined: No authentication on the route, no check on who the caller is, and no conditional on the header. Nothing stops disclosure to any caller. Success also requires a zip that works.
findings.fix: Remove the response header. If the partner must receive the file, make a server-side outbound request that carries the token, and load the token from a secret store or environment, not source. Rotate the exposed token.

findings.title: Request-controlled file name used unsanitised in input and output paths
findings.description: name is placed in both /tmp/<name>.zip and /var/reports/<name>.csv with no normalisation or check for path separators or '..'. Traversal sequences redirect the zip output outside /tmp and let the input resolve to any .csv on the filesystem. The zip contents are not returned to the caller, which limits the impact to file creation and read of .csv files.
findings.attackPath: src/export.js:11 (name = req.query.name) -> src/export.js:12 (path concatenation passed to zip)
findings.exploit: GET /export?name=../../home/svc/x creates /home/svc/x.zip, a zip written outside /tmp, if the process can write there. Described only, never run.
findings.mitigationExamined: No path.basename, path.resolve containment check or allow-list is applied. The fixed .csv and .zip suffixes limit the file types but not the directories.
findings.fix: Allow only a strict token for name (no '/', '\\' or '..'), build paths with path.join and verify the resolved path stays under /var/reports and a dedicated export directory, and generate the zip name server-side.

findings.title: Export endpoint has no authentication and does not tie the report to the caller
findings.description: The comment describes the customer's own cart report, but the report file is selected only by the request's name parameter. There is no authentication in server.js and no ownership check in exportCart, so any caller can request any report, including another customer's.
findings.attackPath: src/server.js:3 (no auth middleware) -> src/export.js:11 (object id from request) -> src/export.js:12 (report for that name read and zipped)
findings.exploit: An anonymous client enumerates report names and triggers export of other customers' reports. Described only, never run.
findings.mitigationExamined: No session, token or policy check exists in server.js or export.js. The response returns the zip file name but not its contents.
findings.fix: Require an authenticated session and derive the report path from the caller's customer id rather than a client-supplied name. Return the file only through an authorised download route.

findings.title: exec error message, including command line and paths, returned to the client
findings.description: On any exec failure the handler sends err.message in a 500 response. For child_process.exec this contains the full command string, the filesystem paths and the tool's stderr, disclosing internal layout and the injected input.
findings.exploit: Send a name for which zip fails to read the full command and /var/reports and /tmp paths in the response body. Described only, never run.
findings.mitigationExamined: No error sanitising or generic message is applied.
findings.fix: Log the error server-side and return a generic 500 body.

findings.title: api: hard-coded live-looking partner API bearer token committed in source (SHA-256 prefix not computed)

The SHA-256 prefix, computed by the session after the hunt, is 99a738e7001e.
findings.attackPath: Anyone with read access to the repository or any clone or fork, such as a contractor, CI log, leaked backup or future public push, can read the token and call the partner API as this service.
findings.exploit: Read the literal from export.js or git history and present it as a bearer credential to the partner API. Not run.

findings.fix: Rotate the token with the partner now. Load it from an environment variable or secret manager. Purge it from history if the repo is shared, and add secret scanning as a pre-commit check.

findings.title: api: partner bearer token is sent back to every caller of GET /export in the Authorization response header
findings.description: exportCart sets res.set('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + PARTNER_API_TOKEN) on the HTTP response to the requester. server.js routes every request to exportCart with no authentication check, so the partner credential is disclosed in the response header.
findings.attackPath: A remote unauthenticated client sends GET /export?name=<x> and reads the Authorization header from the response when the zip step succeeds, gaining the partner credential.
findings.exploit: Issue a request to the export endpoint and read the response headers. Not run.
findings.mitigationExamined: No auth middleware or route check in server.js, no header filtering, and the token is set on the success path only. A proxy in front could strip it, but none is present in the repo.
findings.fix: Remove the Authorization response header. Use the token only on outbound calls to the partner, server side. Rotate the token as in the previous finding.

findings.title: api: setup script pipes a remote installer into sh with no pinning or verification
findings.description: The 'setup' npm script runs setup.sh, which runs curl -fsSL https://get.example-reports.dev/install.sh | sh. The installer content is not pinned to a version, hash or signature.
findings.attackPath: An attacker who compromises or takes over get.example-reports.dev, or who intercepts the connection, serves a malicious install.sh. It runs with the privileges of whoever runs npm run setup on a fresh machine or in a build.
findings.exploit: Serve a modified install.sh from the host. Not run.
findings.mitigationExamined: The script uses HTTPS (-fsSL) and runs only when invoked manually, not from a lifecycle hook such as postinstall or prepare. There is no checksum, signature or version pin, and no CI invokes it in the repo.
findings.fix: Download a versioned artifact, verify its checksum or signature, then run it. Alternatively vendor the installer or use a package from a pinned registry.

findings.title: renderBadge writes unescaped userName into innerHTML
findings.description: badgeHtml concatenates userName into an HTML string with no escaping (line 2), and renderBadge assigns the result to el.innerHTML (line 5). Any markup in the customer's name is parsed as HTML by the browser. No sanitisation or escaping exists anywhere in the web repo.
findings.attackPath: Customer-controlled name (source outside the repo; per tasks/501/501.md the badge shows the customer's name) -> renderBadge(el, userName) src/badge.js:4 -> badgeHtml(userName) src/badge.js:1-2 (string concatenation, no escaping) -> el.innerHTML = ... src/badge.js:5 (HTML sink). No caller exists in the web repo, so the entry point and the audience of the rendered badge are not confirmed.
findings.exploit: A customer sets their name to markup with an event handler, such as an img tag with onerror. When renderBadge renders it, the browser creates the element and runs the handler in the application origin. If the badge is shown to other users, such as staff viewing the customer, this is stored XSS; if only the customer sees their own name, it is self-XSS. Described only, never run.
findings.mitigationExamined: Looked for escaping, a sanitiser, a framework default and a Content-Security-Policy. The repo has no framework, no HTML page, no escape helper and no CSP. src/format.js only trims strings. tests/badge.test.js only asserts the name is present in the output.
findings.fix: Build the node with the DOM: create a span, set className to 'badge', set textContent to userName, then call el.replaceChildren(span). Or HTML-escape &, <, >, " and ' in userName inside badgeHtml. Add a test that a name containing markup is rendered as text.
